title: Shraddha Kapoor Is Unrecognisable — and Now a Political Party Wants to Rename Her Movie
excerpt: The Eetha teaser turned 2 million heads with Shraddha's raw transformation into a legendary Lavani queen. Then Maharashtra's NCP and Vithabai's own family said the title erases the woman it celebrates.
body:
There's a moment in the *Eetha* teaser where you genuinely forget you're looking at Shraddha Kapoor.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=zfopTfY3lBU

She's backstage at a packed Lavani performance, heavily pregnant, drenched in sweat, and the audience is chanting her name. Then she goes into labour. And then — because the woman this film is based on was genuinely built different — she gets back up and finishes the show. The voiceover calls her a *toofan*. That's not hyperbole. That's a description.

The teaser for *Eetha*, directed by Laxman Utekar (*Chhava*, *Mimi*, *Zara Hatke Zara Bachke*) and produced by Dinesh Vijan's Maddock Films, dropped on June 23 and has since racked up over 2.1 million likes on Shraddha's Instagram alone. The film is based on the extraordinary life of Vithabai Narayangaonkar, Maharashtra's legendary Lavani and Tamasha artist — a woman born in 1935 who started performing as a child and became so dominant in her art form that she earned the title *Lavani Samragyi* — Queen of Lavani. She was honoured by the President of India. Twice.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZ6yzfLiODj/

But here's where it gets complicated. The film isn't called *Vithabai*. It's called *Eetha*. And that choice has turned into a full-blown political and cultural controversy less than a week after the teaser went live.

The Revolt

> "Randeep Hooda and Mohammad Zeeshan Ayyub round out the key cast, adding dramatic heft to what already looks like one of the most performance-driven Hindi films of the year."

The Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) was the first to formally object. Babasaheb Patil, Maharashtra State President of the NCP's Film and Cultural Department, publicly questioned why a biopic celebrating one of Maharashtra's most iconic cultural figures doesn't carry her name. The party suggested alternatives — *Vitha*, *Vithabai* — arguing that erasing Vithabai's name from a film about her life does a disservice to her legacy.

Then the family joined in. Vithabai's sons, Kailash and Rajesh Narayangaonkar, and her grandson Mohit, issued a statement supporting the NCP's demand. Their argument is simple and hard to dismiss: if you're telling this woman's story, honour this woman's name. Future generations, they say, should know exactly who they're watching.

As of now, neither Utekar nor Maddock Films has responded publicly. There's no legal order — no trademark or copyright claim has been filed — but the pressure is mounting from cultural groups and the subject's own descendants, the kind of combination that tends to concentrate minds in Bollywood's business offices.

![Maddock Films — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/6/6e/Maddock_Films_logo.jpeg)

The Performance Nobody Is Arguing About

Whatever happens with the title, something else is clear: Shraddha Kapoor has never done anything like this.

The woman who built a career on accessible rom-coms (*Aashiqui 2*, *Stree*) and mass entertainers (*Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar*) is playing a rural folk artist from 1950s Maharashtra — performing Lavani in full traditional costume, pregnant on stage, with a physical intensity that the teaser sells in every frame. This isn't a glamorous biopic where a star plays dress-up for three songs and picks up a Filmfare. This looks like the role of her career.

Randeep Hooda and Mohammad Zeeshan Ayyub round out the key cast, adding dramatic heft to what already looks like one of the most performance-driven Hindi films of the year.

The Bollywood Name Game

This isn't the first time a film's title has sparked a firestorm. Sanjay Leela Bhansali changed *Ram-Leela* to *Goliyon Ki Rasleela Ram-Leela* after religious objections. *Padmaavat* was *Padmavati* before it wasn't. The lesson is always the same: in Indian cinema, a name is never just a name. It carries the weight of community, legacy, and political identity.

But this case is different. There's no allegation of disrespect or distortion — the teaser is clearly reverential. The question is simply whether Vithabai Narayangaonkar deserves to see her own name on the marquee. For her family, the answer is obvious.

Meanwhile, Off Screen

Shraddha has been in the headlines for more than just *Eetha*. A fan-shot video of her watching *Welcome to the Jungle* in a Mumbai cinema with rumoured boyfriend Rahul Mody went viral this week — the couple laughing in their seats, completely unaware they were being filmed. They've been spotted together regularly since 2024, though neither has confirmed the relationship. She's reportedly also attached to *33* and Nikhil Dwivedi's *Naagin*, both in various stages of production.

Where to Watch

*Eetha* is set for theatrical release on August 28, 2026. No OTT window has been announced yet, but with Maddock's strong Netflix relationship (they produced *Stree 2*, *Munjya*, and *Bhediya*), a streaming premiere will likely follow the standard 6-8 week theatrical window. For diaspora audiences, this is one to watch for in Indian cinema halls across the US, UK, and Canada — the kind of performance-driven film that doesn't come along every year.

The teaser is stunning. The controversy is real. And Shraddha Kapoor just announced, in 90 seconds of footage, that she's done playing it safe.
